description: Una plataforma para detectar cambios oceánicos asociados con El Niño e identificar condiciones ambientales potencialmente desfavorables para la fauna marina de Galápagos.
summary: MAREA is an interactive, bilingual marine observatory that turns 22 years of NASA satellite observations into an accessible scientific exploration of the Galápagos Islands. By analyzing sea surface temperature and chlorophyll-a from 2003 to 2024, MAREA helps users investigate ocean variability, El Niño events, and spatial trends across 156 marine sectors. It also connects environmental observations with independently documented impacts on five emblematic marine species, while clearly distinguishing satellite measurements from ecological evidence and communicating statistical uncertainty.
details:
MAREA — Galápagos Marine Observatory is an interactive platform designed to help people investigate how ocean conditions around the Galápagos Islands change over time and what those changes may mean for marine ecosystems.

The challenge

Understanding long-term Earth system trends requires more than looking at a single graph. Satellite observations must be transformed into accessible evidence, and scientific uncertainty must remain visible. In the Galápagos, ocean warming, biological productivity, and El Niño events are especially relevant to understanding ecological vulnerability.

Our solution

MAREA brings together NASA satellite measurements, spatial analysis, climate-event comparisons, and independently documented marine-species evidence in one bilingual, interactive experience.

Its main features include:

  • Ocean Explorer: Monthly sea surface temperature and chlorophyll-a observations, with interactive spatial layers.
  • Climate Detective: Regional and sector-level trend analysis, seasonal patterns, and statistical interpretation.
  • El Niño Timeline: Exploration of historical climate events and their relationship to local ocean conditions.
  • Marine Life: Five Galápagos marine species presented through scientific explanations, photographs, illustrations, and interactive 3D models.
  • Habitat Signals: Ecological context explaining how ocean conditions can affect marine habitats without implying that satellite data directly measure animal populations.
  • Scientific Report: A documented explanation of methods, data, findings, and limitations.

Data and methodology

The observatory uses 264 monthly NASA JPL MUR sea surface temperature observations and 261 NASA Aqua MODIS chlorophyll-a observations, covering 2003–2024. These support 525 monthly spatial layers and analysis across 156 marine sectors.

Long-term trends are examined using seasonal nonparametric methods, with multiple-testing corrections for sector-level comparisons. The application also compares ocean conditions during the 2015–2016 El Niño period with corresponding months from the study record.

The regional estimates are approximately +0.282°C per decade for sea surface temperature and −0.0141 mg/m³ per decade for chlorophyll-a. Neither regional trend reaches conventional statistical significance. No sector-level trends remain significant after the selected multiple-testing correction. MAREA explicitly communicates these findings rather than presenting uncertain results as confirmed trends.

Scientific integrity

Satellite-derived chlorophyll-a is a proxy for ocean phytoplankton conditions, not a direct measurement of fish populations or animal food availability. Biological observations come from independent scientific literature and are not treated as outcomes measured by NASA satellites.

Technology

MAREA was developed with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, interactive scientific visualizations, and browser-based 3D graphics. The application is available in English and Spanish.

Why it matters

MAREA makes Earth observation data more understandable while demonstrating that responsible scientific communication includes uncertainty, limitations, and clearly documented sources.
